General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Google ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing object enrichments: Transform unstructured data into agent-ready context

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1528 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the vast majority of enterprise information is unstructured, locked away in object storage as petabytes of images, PDFs, videos, and audio files.
  • Recent findings suggest that today, we are introducing object enrichments, a fresh Google Cloud Storage capability that uses AI models to automatically extract rich contextual metadata from Cloud Storage objects and saves it in-place as object context, enabling agents to acquire the information needed to make complex business decisions.
  • Industry observers note that “L'Oreal is the 4th largest advertiser in the world, and managing media assets at that scale is complex.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

In a recent development, the vast majority of enterprise information is unstructured, locked away in object storage as petabytes of images, PDFs, videos, and audio files. This data holds the institutional knowledge AI agents need to do business-critical work. But to an agent, a raw object is just bytes it can't reason over. As enterprises start to deploy agents in production, the focus has shifted toward transforming these raw objects into rich, agent-ready context.

Recent findings suggest that today, we are introducing object enrichments, a fresh Google Cloud Storage capability that uses AI models to automatically extract rich contextual metadata from Cloud Storage objects and saves it in-place as object context, enabling agents to acquire the information needed to make complex business decisions. Object enrichments gives customers access to the AI models used by internal Google services such as Google Photos, offering image annotations like object detection and image labeling at 75% cost savings when compared to similar services from other cloud providers. Available in preview, this fully managed service also includes high-quality PDF classification model, enabling customers to seamlessly turn their object store into an intelligent, AI-ready foundation.

Industry observers note that “L'Oreal is the 4th largest advertiser in the world, and managing media assets at that scale is complex. Cloud Storage object enrichments’s high quality and cost-effective annotations enable us to discover, understand, and govern our content at scale, accelerating marketing and advertising operations while remaining compliant in all markets. Object enrichments enables L'Oreal to label its extensive creative asset repository 100x faster at a fraction of the cost of existing pipelines and processes.” – Antoine Castex, Principal Data & AI Architect, L’Oreal.

To operate efficiently, agents need grounded knowledge; however, reading every raw file at scale is cost- and performance-prohibitive. For example, if an operations agent needs to pinpoint a specific event—such as a doorstep package delivery or a roadway hazard—streaming thousands of smart-camera or vehicle frames into the AI model on every user prompt would burn through expensive tokens and add minutes of delay. To bridge this gap, teams must pre-process raw data and extract rich, contextual metadata, which agents can then leverage at runtime. Historically, achieving this meant dealing with three challenges:.

Cost: Running models over millions to billions of objects is expensive, pushing organizations to compromise and process only a fraction of their data, creating blind spots that lessen agents’ accuracy.

It has been revealed that operational toil: A self-managed pipeline means stitching together multiple services — from event triggers and queues to custom infrastructure built on Cloud Run or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) — along with scalable retry/error logic and job scheduling. Once deployed, that infrastructure still requires continuous upgrades and capacity management. Teams sometimes spend months on this plumbing rather than focusing on building agents that solve actual business problems.

It has been revealed that fragmented metadata: Extracted metadata often lands in a separate data store, decoupling context from the bytes it describes. Teams must pay for and maintain a second storage system, govern access policies across disconnected permission models, and run custom cleanup jobs to keep metadata in sync when source objects are copied, moved, or deleted.

This is why we built object enrichments: to natively provide agent-ready context for your unstructured data, equipping your agents with complete, grounded knowledge without prohibitive costs, custom pipeline plumbing, or fragmented metadata.

According to recent reports, 1. Reduce costs with Google modelsObject enrichments offers dramatic savings at scale: enriching 10 million images or PDFs costs just $700 (according to published pricing). You can use Google’s high-quality AI models for image annotations—including object detection, face detection, image labeling, and explicit content detection—at one of the industry’s best price points. In addition, the PDF classification model lets you categorize documents into standard business and industry categories like Finance, Games, News, and Health.

"Even with a highly accurate baseline, Hyperscience leveraged object enrichments to drive a 50%+ lift in document classification accuracy, while simultaneously reducing classification inference costs by 2-3x.” – Mayur Pillay, VP Partnerships, Hyperscience.

2. Generate richer context with GeminiFor complex multimodal reasoning across text, PDFs, images, audio, and video, you can leverage Gemini natively with object enrichments, unlocking advanced use cases such as summarization, entity extraction, transcription, and translation. Please reach out to us at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to this upcoming functionality.

3. No pipeline, low toil setupSkip the brittle, multi-component DIY pipelines. Setting up an enrichment job just takes three simple steps, with no code required in the Google Cloud console, or programmatically via the Cloud Storage API, following these steps:.

It has been revealed that define your scope: Provide a set of buckets containing the objects to process and specify the processing location. Object enrichments can scale to millions or billions of objects.

Choose your models: Pick one or more of the five first-party Cloud Storage models for images and PDFs.

Grant permissions: Grant the necessary IAM permissions to the object enrichments service to access your Cloud Storage buckets.

According to recent reports, object enrichments handles the rest: It orchestrates model inference, parses the responses, and writes the results to each object's object context, with built-in retries and throttling. There are no queues to manage, workers to scale, or glue code to maintain.

"Cloud Storage object enrichments and BigQuery, slashes AI development from 6 months to 1 month while rapidly improving our models." - Brandon Bunker, VP of Product AI, Vivint.

According to recent reports, 4. Context lives where the bytes liveInstead of parking metadata in a separate data store, object enrichments writes model outputs directly to object context, a specialized Cloud Storage metadata construct that’s purpose-built for storing contextual information as structured key-value pairs alongside the object itself. Because context is stored alongside object’s actual bytes, you get enterprise-grade data management out of the box, with:.

Recent findings suggest that cloud Storage durability and simplified lifecycle management: Object context shares the same durability and consistency properties as the underlying Cloud Storage object. It travels automatically with the object during copy, move, and replication operations and is automatically removed when the object is deleted — no more cleanup jobs!

Fine-grained IAM governance: Using IAM, administrators can control who can read, add, update, or remove object context.

Fast object filtering and serving: Applications can filter object listings directly by object context key-value pairs or read context metadata alongside objects, in order to serve richer experiences.

Turnkey multimodal analytics in BigQuery: You can easily configure your object context to natively flow into BigQuery via Storage Insights datasets, allowing data teams to run SQL analytics, build dashboards, and join unstructured file insights with structured enterprise tables, without writing a single line of ETL code.

Early customers are already putting object enrichments to work across key business scenarios:.

Industry observers note that creative asset search and media archives: Marketing, retail, and media organizations manage petabytes of creative image assets, where finding a specific asset, e.g., "a red car driving at sunset" or "a vintage convertible in the desert during golden hour", requires rich semantic metadata. Object enrichments automatically generates descriptive labels in object context, which can then be indexed into a vector database or BigQuery to power accurate retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications and asset-discovery agents.

Automated trust, safety, and content moderation: Social platforms, marketplaces, and digital media pipelines scan millions of user uploads and supplier catalogs every day for explicit content. Historically, scaling this for every single upload has been cost-prohibitive, but not anymore. With object enrichments, you can process 10 million images for just $700.

Training data curation for frontier AI: Autonomous driving, smart home, and robotics companies capture hundreds of millions of raw camera and sensor files. They often need targeted data samples for specific fine-tuning scenarios, which make up only a tiny fraction of their corpus. By enriching raw captures in place with object detection and image labeling models and then querying the resulting metadata in BigQuery, ML engineers can pinpoint exact training cohorts in minutes rather than months.

Multimodal analytics: Combine insights from images and documents with structured business data to drive personalization, fraud detection, and trend discovery — for example, analyzing customer uploaded images of the product alongside their comments and recent sales data.

In a recent development, object enrichments is available in preview today in the Cloud Storage console and through the Cloud Storage API. To get started, check out the following resources.

Read the documentation: Learn how to configure an enrichments job and use object contexts.

Analyze in BigQuery: Set up Storage Insights datasets and query your enrichments alongside your BigQuery business data.

Connect your agents: Pair object enrichments and object context with the Cloud Storage MCP server to give agents secure, IAM-scoped access to your data and its context.

Review pricing: See Cloud Storage pricing for details.

Gemini enrichments: Reach out to us at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to this upcoming functionality.

Start building: Head to the Cloud Storage console to enrich your first bucket in just three clicks.

PRC-linked influence operations are targeting AI debates in the US

📅 10 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (449 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity.
  • In this report, we describe two clusters of ChatGPT accounts likely originating from China that we banned after they used our models in support of apparent covert influence operations that promoted narratives in an attempt to manipulate a legitimate debate about American AI and wider tech policies.
  • It has been revealed that the first cluster generated social media comments and images claiming that data center buildouts for AI were increasing electricity prices for average families.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. We advance this mission by deploying our innovations to build democratic AI: AI shaped by democratic principles, governed by common-sense rules and designed to help people solve hard problems while protecting them from real harm. That mission also requires identifying and disrupting attempts by authoritarian regimes and their proxies to use AI systems to coerce critics, surveil communities or covertly interfere in democratic societies.

In this report, we describe two clusters of ChatGPT accounts likely originating from China that we banned after they used our models in support of apparent covert influence operations that promoted narratives in an attempt to manipulate a legitimate debate about American AI and wider tech policies.

It has been revealed that the first cluster generated social media comments and images claiming that data center buildouts for AI were increasing electricity prices for average families. We named this cluster the “Data Center Bandwagon” campaign.

The second cluster generated comments and images criticizing US tariffs as attempts to dominate technological competition and specified in their prompts that the content should not include China’s leader Xi Jinping in the output and instead include only President Trump. This cluster was connected to a network of likely inauthentic social media accounts that were also likely targeting OpenAI by claiming ChatGPT user data had been compromised. These allegations were entirely false. We named this second cluster the “Tech and Tariffs” campaign.

In a recent development, the targeting of OpenAI and US data center buildouts is significant not because the operation appears to have shifted public opinion, but because it reveals PRC-origin influence operators testing narratives against AI infrastructure – a foundation of US technological leadership, economic growth and the broader democratic AI ecosystem. The operation sought to exploit and amplify existing public concerns about energy prices and local impacts of data center development, but we found no evidence of meaningful breakout beyond its own activity. Foreign influence operations have long sought to latch onto existing local problems and sincerely held beliefs, using them to build credibility, amplify divisions or exacerbate public distrust. In this case, the operators attempted to covertly insert themselves into an ongoing American debate about the future of the country’s AI capabilities while hiding who they were and what motivated them.

By publishing these findings, we aim to help our industry, governments, civil society and the public better identify and disrupt attempts by foreign threat actors to manipulate legitimate public debates, weaken democratic institutions and advance totalitarianism with AI characteristics - the use of AI for surveillance, censorship and control over political, social and private life.

Recent findings suggest that founded in 1857, BBVA is a global financial institution supporting people and businesses across Europe, Mexico, South America, Turkey, and the U.S., serving tens of millions of customers worldwide. After pioneering digital and mobile banking over the last decade, BBVA is now entering a newly introduced phase: transforming banking around artificial intelligence.

Industry observers note that to accelerate that transformation, BBVA and OpenAI have formed a strategic collaboration designed to integrate AI across customer experiences, operations, software development, and the day-to-day work of employees throughout the organization. The collaboration marks a new level of partnership between a global financial institution and OpenAI, with teams from both companies working together on shared priorities and long-term transformation initiatives.

By the end of 2025, that collaboration had evolved into a broader strategic alliance centered around "The Eight," BBVA's AI transformation roadmap for redesigning banking end-to-end—from customer experience and commercial banking to risk, operations, software development, and employee productivity.

Rather than approaching AI as a standalone technology initiative, BBVA is rethinking how the bank operates across every layer of the organization: how customers interact with financial services, how employees make decisions, how risk is analyzed, and how operations are executed at scale.

The initiative spans every layer of the bank: from AI-powered financial assistants capable of anticipating customer needs, to tools that help bankers and risk analysts make faster and more informed decisions, to systems that automate operations and accelerate software development across the organization.

Through the collaboration, OpenAI is working closely with BBVA teams across engineering, research, product development, and operations to help develop and scale these AI capabilities securely across a global banking organization.

The relationship between BBVA and OpenAI began in 2024 with an initial deployment of ChatGPT Enterprise to 3,000 employees across multiple countries and business areas. As adoption accelerated organically, BBVA expanded access across the organization.

Today more than 100,000 employees globally use ChatGPT Enterprise, making BBVA one of the largest enterprise adopters of generative AI in the financial sector.

Industry observers note that teams across legal, risk, engineering, operations, finance, marketing, and customer service integrated ChatGPT into everyday workflows. The deployment demonstrated how generative AI could scale securely inside a highly regulated organization while delivering measurable operational impact across the business.

In a recent development, for a highly regulated global bank, scaling AI required more than simply deploying licenses. BBVA built its AI adoption strategy around three core pillars: trust, governance, and structured learning. From the beginning, BBVA aligned security, legal, compliance, and technology teams to ensure employees had access to trusted AI tools within clear governance frameworks.

Rather than allowing unauthorized experimentation with consumer AI tools, the bank chose to provide employees with secure enterprise-grade access and formal enablement programs.

To support adoption at scale, BBVA created a structured enablement framework that included an organization-wide AI champions network, along with advanced consumers known internally as AI “wizards.” These teams lead hands-on workshops, help colleagues integrate ChatGPT into everyday workflows, and identify valuable use cases across the organization.

Leadership participation became a major accelerator for adoption. BBVA provided specific training to 250 leaders, including the CEO and chairman, and today members of the executive committee are among the company's most active ChatGPT users.

Once employees began seeing practical value in their daily work, adoption expanded organically across the company.

Industry observers note that as adoption expanded, employees across BBVA began building custom GPTs tailored to specialized workflows across legal, risk, customer service, finance, and marketing. To date, employees have created more than 20,000 GPTs across the organization, with approximately 4,000 used frequently by teams around the world.

Recent findings suggest that in credit risk, BBVA developed Credit Analysis Pro GPT, which accelerates assessments by extracting and analyzing unstructured data from annual reports, ESG disclosures, and media coverage—work that was previously manual and time-intensive. By automating these tasks, analysts can focus more on strategic analysis and higher-value work, including how ESG factors are incorporated into risk models.

Recent findings suggest that in legal services, BBVA created a Retail Banking Legal Assistant GPT to help respond to approximately 40,000 annual client-related legal inquiries received from branch managers. The GPT drafts responses by pulling from multiple internal knowledge sources, dramatically reducing manual research time for the nine-person legal team.

In Mexico, a Client Experience Assistant GPT analyzes thousands of open-ended customer survey responses, accelerating sentiment analysis, surfacing key themes, and recommending actions that help improve customer experience faster and at scale.

In Peru, more than 3,000 employees now use an internal AI assistant that has reduced average query handling times from approximately 7.5 minutes to around 1 minute—an efficiency improvement of roughly 80%.

These examples illustrate a broader shift underway at BBVA. What began as employee productivity gains is increasingly becoming a foundation for how the bank delivers services, makes decisions, and scales expertise across the organization.

100,000 employees using ChatGPT Enterprise globally.

~3 hours saved per employee, per week.

Employee-led AI adoption across business functions.

8 major transformation initiatives under “The Eight”.

Treat AI as business transformation: BBVA approached AI as a redesign of customer experience, operations, and ways of working across the organization — not as a standalone innovation effort.

Build with domain expertise: The collaboration combines OpenAI’s frontier AI capabilities with BBVA’s deep expertise in banking, risk, operations, and customer experience.

Scale securely from day one: Transforming a global financial institution with AI requires governance, data architecture, and security frameworks designed to scale across the organization.

Empower employees with AI: By extending AI capabilities broadly across the workforce, BBVA is enabling employees to become active participants in the bank’s transformation.

Train leadership early: AI adoption accelerates when senior leaders actively use the technology themselves. Early training programs for executives — including the CEO and chairman — help establish AI as a strategic priority across the organization.

Move from reactive to proactive banking: The long-term ambition is not simply greater efficiency, but a more intelligent and personalized banking experience capable of anticipating customer needs.

For BBVA, ChatGPT Enterprise adoption is only one part of a much larger transformation. Through "The Eight," the bank is pursuing a long-term vision for redesigning banking around AI—from customer engagement and commercial banking to risk, operations, software development, and employee productivity.

In a recent development, working closely with OpenAI, BBVA is continuing to explore how AI can help create a more proactive, intelligent, and personalized banking experience while improving how work gets done across the organization. The goal is not simply to deploy AI tools, but to rethink how a global bank operates in an AI-native era.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Today we’re announcing that OpenAI will acquire Ona⁠(opens in a newly introduced window), bringing its secure cloud execution and orchestration technology into our rapidly expanding Codex ecosystem.
  • It has been revealed that more than 5 million people use Codex each week to research, analyze, build, and automate their work—up 400% from earlier this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Expands Codex with secure, customer-controlled cloud infrastructure for long-running agents across software and knowledge work.

Today we’re announcing that OpenAI will acquire Ona⁠(opens in a newly introduced window), bringing its secure cloud execution and orchestration technology into our rapidly expanding Codex ecosystem.

It has been revealed that more than 5 million people use Codex each week to research, analyze, build, and automate their work—up 400% from earlier this year. Codex began as a tool for software developers and now helps a wider range of people do complex work from an initial request through to a finished result.

As Codex becomes more capable, its most valuable work is unfolding over hours or days, rather than minutes. We believe people should be able to delegate more ambitious work without remaining tied to the machine where it began. The work should continue beyond the initial session, with Codex making it possible to stay connected and check progress, provide direction, make decisions, and review results from anywhere.

Ona will help us do that. Its technology provides secure, persistent environments where agents can access the tools, systems, and context they need to make progress over time.

By bringing Ona to OpenAI, we will expand Codex beyond work tied to a single device or active session and help more organizations deploy agents securely in production.

Recent findings suggest that ona has spent years helping developers move software development from local machines into the cloud. The manufacturer has helped 2 million developers work in secure, reproducible cloud environments and supports multiple shared customers.

That experience is directly relevant to the next phase of Codex, enabling agents to continue working inside a customer’s cloud environment even when laptops are closed.

Industry observers note that as organizations move from experimenting with agents to deploying them across production workflows, capable models are only one part of what they need.Organizations should be able to give people the benefits of persistent agentic work with confidence, knowing agents are operating inside environments that meet their security, governance, and operational requirements. That means having control over where they run, what they can access, how credentials are scoped, how activity is logged, and how work moves through review.

Ona’s customer-controlled execution model will allow agents to operate inside an organization’s own cloud environment while OpenAI provides the intelligence and orchestration that power the experience. This gives organizations greater control over their infrastructure, data, and security boundaries without limiting what Codex can accomplish.

The acquisition is subject to customary closing conditions, including receipt of required regulatory approvals. Until closing, OpenAI and Ona will remain separate and independent companies.

After closing, the Ona team will join OpenAI and work with the Codex team to advance secure, persistent enterprise execution capabilities and help scale Codex to more enterprises worldwide.

We’re excited to welcome the Ona team to OpenAI as we build AI systems that help people and businesses create and accomplish more while meeting the security and control requirements of real-world deployment. Together, we will help engineering teams safely take on sustained work across the software lifecycle, from running tests and resolving problems to modernizing applications, addressing vulnerabilities, and supporting complex workflows over time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI announces support for the EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated content, building on years of provenance work.

According to recent reports, people are using AI to create and edit content in latest ways. As these tools become more capable and more widely used, people should have context about the content they see online.

Sources indicate that today, following publication of the European Commission’s Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content⁠(opens in a fresh window), OpenAI is announcing its support for the Code and the ambition behind it. The Code is an crucial step in implementing the EU AI Act and building a more transparent digital ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that our support builds on years of internal research, product development, and cooperation with the wider ecosystem to strengthen provenance for AI-generated content. OpenAI has been developing and adopting provenance standards since 2024, when we began adding C2PA metadata to our DALL-E 3 image generation tool. Since then, we have continued to strengthen provenance through improved marking and detection methods, upcoming research, and the release of our first public verification tool. Drawing on years of expertise, we contributed to the development of this Code alongside hundreds of other stakeholders to help ensure a trustworthy AI ecosystem.

This builds on our broader approach to AI governance in Europe. In 2025, OpenAI was the first US company to sign the EU’s General-Purpose AI Code of Practice⁠(opens in a new window), reflecting our belief that clear, workable rules can help AI develop responsibly while giving companies the certainty to keep building. We support this new Code in the same spirit. Advancing transparency of AI-generated content is an ecosystem-wide effort, requiring contribution from actors all along the value chain. The EU AI Act and the Code recognize this, and we are committed to doing our part by complying with the requirements that apply to our relevant products.

Sources indicate that as AI tools become a part of how people build, imagine, and share, it’s important that people can understand where content comes from and interpret it with confidence. Provenance signals can help by giving people context about content’s source, how it was created or edited, and whether it is what it claims to be. Provenance can also help protect the digital ecosystem by making it easier to detect disinformation campaigns and support election integrity.

Sources indicate that effective, reliable and robust provenance methods should be built collectively and work across the ecosystem. That is why we work with coalitions like C2PA, which brings together news organizations, device manufacturers, online platforms, and AI providers to advance interoperable standards. C2PA metadata is an key foundation for provenance. It helps content carry information about where it came from, how it was created or edited, and who signed that information. But metadata is not foolproof. It can be stripped, lost through uploads and downloads, or broken by transformations like file format changes, resizing, or screenshots.

Industry observers note that to make provenance more resilient, OpenAI takes a multi-layered approach that combines different signals, product safeguards, and collaboration across the wider ecosystem. Our current work includes:.

C2PA Content Credentials⁠(opens in a upcoming window) for images: We began adding C2PA metadata to images created and edited by DALL·E 3 in ChatGPT and the OpenAI API, and have continued expanding provenance signals across OpenAI-generated images.

Industry observers note that multiple signals for OpenAI-generated images: Images generated with ChatGPT, Codex, and the OpenAI API include both C2PA metadata and SynthID watermarks. Metadata can carry richer information, while watermarking can help preserve a signal across contexts.

A public verification experience: openai.com/verify lets people check whether supported images contain provenance signals associated with OpenAI-generated images.

Contributions to open standards. In 2024, OpenAI joined the C2PA Steering Committee, a cross-industry effort involving software companies, camera manufacturers, media organizations, and online platforms.

Product safeguards: Provenance complements policies, classifiers, reporting channels, and enforcement processes that reduce deceptive uses of AI-generated content, including likeness misuse and election-related deception.

While provenance is useful, it is still a nascent field. Signals can be lost as content moves online: metadata can be removed, watermarks can degrade, and labels only help where people encounter content. Advancing the reliability, robustness and interoperability of provenance techniques still requires significant work and cooperation among the ecosystem.

Sources indicate that the Code of Practice sets the right direction: a high level of ambition to advance provenance techniques. As it is implemented, it should stay grounded in methods that work in practice and flexible enough to reflect the limitations of current techniques.

OpenAI will keep strengthening content transparency across our products, contributing to the development of interoperable standards, and improving verification tools. We look forward to working with the AI Office, Member States, and the wider AI community to build a safer, more transparent AI ecosystem.

Tech Report: The Blueprint: How Kult built a gaming companion that actually knows your game

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1323 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, welcome to The Blueprint, our ongoing series where we highlight how Google Cloud customers are tackling unique and common challenges across industries using the latest AI and cloud technologies.
  • Kult is a London-based startup building a companion experience for games.
  • It has been revealed that traditionally, getting help in the middle of a game meant alt-tabbing, opening a video, scrolling a forum, and hoping you find the answer before you forget why you looked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

According to recent reports, welcome to The Blueprint, our ongoing series where we highlight how Google Cloud customers are tackling unique and common challenges across industries using the latest AI and cloud technologies. We hope to inspire others looking to innovate in their work.

Kult is a London-based startup building a companion experience for games. It sits alongside your session, understands the game you are playing and where you are in it, and answers by voice and on a second screen. The more you play with it, the better it knows how you like to play.

It has been revealed that traditionally, getting help in the middle of a game meant alt-tabbing, opening a video, scrolling a forum, and hoping you find the answer before you forget why you looked. Information should come to the player instead. As gamers ourselves, our team wanted a way for someone to be able to ask a question out loud, hands on the keyboard or controller, hear an answer, and consult a second screen if needed, without interrupting their immersion in the game.

Three things decide whether that works: latency, accuracy and cost.

Industry observers note that latency: Games are time-sensitive. The answer has to be fast, and the interaction should feel like asking a friend who’s an expert on the game, sitting on the couch next to you and watching you play.

Sources indicate that accuracy: General-purpose models have training cutoffs. They can be months out of date and are often wrong about a specific game, patch, or build — and a wrong answer can be costly in the game and a waste of the player's time. Every game also has its own items, systems, and vocabulary, so accuracy has to hold across hundreds of games. The right answer also depends on the player: The same question deserves a different answer 10 minutes into a game than a 100 hours in.

Cost: An always-on companion handles many turns per session, so every turn has to be inexpensive enough for a consumer product. Covering hundreds of games is only possible if adding one is cheap and takes no manual work.

Given these needs, we knew we would want a range of models to build Kult. Fortunately, Google’s Gemini models have some of the greatest variety in terms of balancing performance and especially cost, and with the Model Garden in Gemini platform, we have access to hundreds of models beyond Gemini. Gemini models have became the default family on both sides of the system: the live conversation, and the knowledge behind it, dynamically match the right model for every task.

Sources indicate that the lightest Gemini Flash tier handles high-volume, repetitive work, where we make thousands of small calls for every game we add. Gemini Flash runs every conversational turn. It works out what the player is asking and writes an answer grounded in our knowledge of that game, fast enough to keep up with play. The latest and most advanced Gemini models handle the rare, heavy reasoning we do once per game.

Sources indicate that having that range on one API surface matters to a small team. The latest Gemini Flash models in particular sit at a point of price, speed, and quality that we have not found elsewhere, and they are the reason an always-on gaming companion works as a consumer product.

In a recent development, we reach the models through both the Gemini platform and the Gemini Developer API, with a routing layer that picks the backend for each model. Our backend runs on Google Kubernetes Engine.

Sources indicate that every answer comes in two parts. The voice gives the short version. At the same moment, a visual answer lands in a feed on the player's second screen: images, embedded video, maps, builds, interactive tools made for that game, and links to the guides and creators behind the answer.

It has been revealed that we build that feed with Google's open standard for agent-generated interfaces. The model does not write code. It describes the interface it wants using a catalog of components we designed, and the app renders it natively in Kult's own style. That keeps the feed safe and consistent, and lets us add fresh kinds of visual answers, and new devices, without rebuilding the front end.

Kult now covers more than 100 games, and adding a game is an automated process, not a manual project. That’s a key part of what lets a small team aim at any game a player picks up, including new releases, where most of the playing happens in the first weeks.

In a recent development, we are in alpha with our first players and opening up to more over the coming months. As we have grown, we have built a close working relationship with the Google Cloud team, with direct access to their engineers when we need it. That matters when every model generation raises the ceiling of what a gaming companion product can do.

This expertise, both within the models and our supportive partners, allows us to focus on our passion: building the features gamers want, faster and better than any possible competition.

Five principles shape how Kult works.

Sources indicate that answers come from knowledge we build, not from what a model happens to remember. A game can change with every patch. For each game we cover, Kult builds a structured knowledge base automatically and keeps it current, and the model's job is to reason over that knowledge.

The answer depends on who is asking. Kult keeps track of your session: the game, what you have been doing, and what you asked a moment ago. "What is he weak to?" needs no further explanation, because Kult already knows which boss you’re facing. Over time it learns from how you play, what you ask about and what you ignore, and shapes its answers around you. A player who wants the fastest route and one who wants to find everything should not get the same replies.

In a recent development, the player is never left in silence. Kult responds straight away and carries the conversation while the deeper reasoning runs behind it. The spoken answer is short, and the visual feed carries everything the voice cannot.

The smallest model that can do the job does the job. Much of the work in a system like ours is a decision, not a piece of writing. It needs to understand which game the query is about, does the question need a lookup, did the answer cover the point.

Sources indicate that for decisions like these we use Jev, a decision-only model that returns a choice with a calibrated confidence score. Confident cases are settled in a fraction of a second at a fraction of the cost, and uncertain ones escalate to a larger Gemini model. Every model sits behind a registry, so when a new generation ships, we benchmark it against reference answers written by people who know the games, and swap it in if it wins.

According to recent reports, every question makes Kult better. Taken together, the questions players ask about a game show us where its knowledge is thin and what to build next. We are designing Kult so that this loop tightens with every session. The more people play, the richer the knowledge becomes for everyone. Every session teaches a player something, as well as the entire Kult system, and Kult helps them keep it. We think the companion that sits beside the game is only the start.

Next is computer vision. In the coming months, Kult will start to see what is happening in your game, so the companion can be aware of the moment without being asked. We’re using Google's Live models as part of that work, for video understanding and more.

If you are a gamer, try it for yourself www.joinkult.gg.

How an astrophysicist uses Codex to help simulate black holes

📅 11 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Codex helps Chi-kwan Chan to refine and test algorithms that simulate the movement of electrons and ions around a black hole.
  • According to recent reports, the gravity around a black hole is so extreme that nothing, not even light, can escape once it gets close enough.
  • With Codex, Chan—a researcher at the University of Arizona and Steward Observatory—is tackling this problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Codex helps Chi-kwan Chan to refine and test algorithms that simulate the movement of electrons and ions around a black hole.

According to recent reports, the gravity around a black hole is so extreme that nothing, not even light, can escape once it gets close enough. Astrophysicists like Chi-kwan Chan study black holes with computer simulations and observations. But current algorithms and computing power limit how realistic those simulations can be.

With Codex, Chan—a researcher at the University of Arizona and Steward Observatory—is tackling this problem.

In a recent development, black holes are among the best places to test Einstein’s general theory of relativity, he stated. The theory is presently our best explanation of gravity: instead of a force pulling objects together, gravity is the result of mass and energy bending the fabric of space and time.

Chan is part of the international Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration, which published the first image of a black hole in 2019. The team is at the moment gathering observations to produce the first video of a supermassive black hole, focusing on the one at the center of the M87 galaxy.

But turning observations into scientific understanding requires enormous amounts of data processing, large-scale computing workflows, and simulations capable of modeling some of the most extreme physics in the universe.

According to recent reports, since light can’t escape a black hole, scientists instead study the region around it called the event horizon, a boundary beyond which matter can’t escape. “It’s a surface of no return,” noted Chan. Matter swirling just outside this boundary emits light that astrophysicists can see, measure, and simulate.

According to recent reports, the 2019 image released by the EHT indicated a black hole’s shadow embedded in glowing plasma near the event horizon. Chan helped develop the simulation and computing tools the team used to interpret the observations. Since then, Chan and his colleagues have continued improving their instruments and observing capabilities as the team moves from still images toward videos.

A short video generated by a supercomputer simulation showing the movement of plasma around the black hole at the center of the Milky Way galaxy.

Credit: EHT Theory Working Group / CK Chan.

Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest roadblocks for Chan and his team is modeling the plasma around black holes. Plasma is superheated matter made up of electrically charged electrons and ions.

In many simulations, scientists simplify plasma by treating it like a fluid, using well-known equations to model its movement around a black hole. That works reasonably well in denser plasma where the electrons and ions constantly collide with each other.

But near the supermassive black holes that Chan and his colleagues are studying, some regions become so hot and diffuse that particles rarely encounter each other. “They don’t really collide with each other,” he said. Instead, the particles mostly spiral around magnetic field lines.

To model that behavior correctly, researchers need to follow trillions of electrons and ions as they rapidly corkscrew around a black hole. Standard simulations must calculate every tiny turn, forcing computers to take extremely small timesteps.

As a result, even the world’s fastest supercomputers can spend most of their time calculating these minuscule particle motions instead of simulating the larger behavior scientists actually want to study.

“For decades, this has limited how realistically we can simulate black hole plasma,” Chan mentioned.

Using AI to build a better digital twin.

Recent findings suggest that chan suspected that latest mathematical techniques could help work around some of these limitations. The basic idea was to change, mathematically, how the simulation tracked particle motion so the computer no longer had to follow every tiny spiral directly.

According to recent reports, “But exploring all the mathematical possibilities by hand would have taken an enormous amount of time,” Chan stated. So he turned to Codex to help derive candidate algorithms and test them against known solutions.

Sources indicate that codex generated many potential approaches—not all of them correct. “But that’s okay,” Chan said. “Most scientific ideas fail. What matters is that these algorithms are testable. Once you find one that works, it can potentially unlock simulations that were previously impossible.”.

Some AI systems can return results without showing the steps they used to produce their conclusions. But Chan’s group uses Codex to propose and implement numerical schemes that they can inspect, test, and understand physically.

Large language models still make mistakes, and many scientists remain cautious about using AI in research. But Chan believes science may be one of the best uses for today’s AI systems precisely because scientific ideas can be tested rigorously.

Recent findings suggest that “We don’t accept an idea because it came from Einstein, from a bright student, or from an AI model,” he mentioned. “We accept it only after repeated testing.”.

Chan sees AI as a tool that can help researchers explore more ideas, test them faster, and accelerate discovery while remaining grounded in verification and reproducibility.

Sources indicate that if the approaches that Chan is testing with Codex succeed, the new algorithms could eventually allow scientists to simulate trillions of particles around black holes. That would enable researchers to study physics that has remained out of reach for decades.

#28836. How to simplify cloud access with Unified Access Policies, now in preview

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1194 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Google ↗ Open Full Page

How to simplify cloud access with Unified Access Policies, now in preview

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1194 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As organizations scale their cloud footprint to thousands of autonomous agents and microservices, you can accidentally create an operational bottleneck with strict Identity and Access Management (IAM).
  • In a recent development, enter Unified Access Policies (UAPs), Google Cloud's next-generation access control engine in Cloud IAM, now in preview at no additional cost.
  • This approach allows you to author a policy once and bind it across your organization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

As organizations scale their cloud footprint to thousands of autonomous agents and microservices, you can accidentally create an operational bottleneck with strict Identity and Access Management (IAM). Meanwhile, administrators still need to enforce least privilege across thousands of resources without slowing down engineering velocity.

In a recent development, enter Unified Access Policies (UAPs), Google Cloud's next-generation access control engine in Cloud IAM, now in preview at no additional cost. UAP consolidates allow and deny rules into one unified schema, and decouples policy definition from resource enforcement.

This approach allows you to author a policy once and bind it across your organization. UAP governs human, workload, and first-class agent identities with your existing IAM policies. With UAP, you can radically simplify your access policies and manage them more easily at scale.

Traditional access policy models can push teams into a tough trade-off between Zero Trust access and pipeline speed due to three compounding forces:.

Fragmented schemas and permission sprawl: In granting thousands of granular permissions across cloud resources, administrators are forced to choose between either over-granting permissions from coarse roles with broad access, or wrangling two different syntaxes (APIs and mental models across allow and deny) just to define one workload's custom access posture.

According to recent reports, policies treated as snowflakes: Because legacy policies attach directly to individual resources, applying a standard developer or security baseline across 25 projects means duplicating and maintaining 50 separate allow and deny policy configurations in Terraform. This approach can create severe configuration fatigue and operational burden, with greater risk of misconfiguration.

In a recent development, scale ceilings and explosion of agent identities: Modern cloud environments span human teams, federated workloads, service accounts, and autonomous agents that should never share generic service account credentials. As non-human and agent identities multiply, large enterprises routinely hit the hard 64 KB single-policy size limit on allow policies — requiring policy refactoring to onboard fresh teams or agents.

Helping platform and security teams address these access limitations demands a upcoming approach: an agent-ready engine on a unified control plane, designed to simplify, centralize, and scale access control.

In a recent development, UAP removes cognitive burden for platform and IAM administrators, security architects, and agent administrators while shrinking your Infrastructure as Code footprint. UAP re-architects how policies are authored, bound, and enforced across your resource hierarchy because it’s built around a simpler authorization model.

1. Unified allow and deny syntax: Consolidate positive access grants and firm security guardrails into a single, auditable policy instead of reconciling separate allow and deny files.

2. Multi-binding support: A standalone policy binding acts as the connective tissue between your policy definition and target Cloud Resource Manager (CRM) nodes (organization, folder, and project). You can now bind a single UAP policy across up to 25 CRM targets in preview, eliminating duplicate Terraform blocks.

Industry observers note that 3. Expanded scale limits (5x effective policy size): UAP breaks through the legacy single-policy size ceiling by letting you attach up to five UAP policies (64 KB and up to 100 rules each) to any single CRM resource — scaling to 2,500 unique principals and 500 groups per resource.

Industry observers note that 4. Clear separation of concerns: Central security architects can author vetted baseline and guardrail policies at the organization node and delegate self-service binding to folder and project administrators, without letting local teams alter central rule logic.

Sources indicate that 5. Expressive permission wildcards and immutable guardrails: Replace brittle permission lists with prefix, suffix, and substring wildcards alongside predefined roles and action exclusions (excluded permissions).

According to recent reports, 6. Built-in readiness for agents: UAP treats agents as first-class principals (principal://agents.global...) rather than generic service accounts. Agent administrators can scope least-privilege allow and deny rules directly to individual agents or entire agent pools, combine UAP with short-lived, downscoped tokens, and build on an extensible foundation for human-in-the-loop and delegated agent authorization.

7. Day 1 parity across all four surfaces: At runtime, Cloud IAM evaluates your existing allow policies, deny policies and UAP policies concurrently across your resource hierarchy. Whether your teams prefer interactive workflows or declarative automation, UAP launches with full create, read, patch, and delete parity across the Google Cloud console, gCloud CLI, Terraform, and the Cloud IAM v3 REST API.

You can deploy your first policy to bring these powerful capabilities into your environment in just a few minutes.

While you can automate UAP through Terraform, gCloud CLI or REST API, you can also author and bind policies interactively in the Google Cloud console.

Step 1: Open the Unified Access Policies tabIn the Google Cloud console, select your target organization, folder, or project in the resource picker and navigate to IAM & Admin > IAM.

Alongside the existing Principals tab, select the new Unified Access Policies tab to view all policies in your scope — including their binding status, governed principals and rule types — and click + Create policy.

Unified Access Policies page lists all the policies managed at/ enforced at the scope picked by the customer (Project, Folder or Org).

Step 2: Define policy details and access rulesIn the Policy Details pane, enter a policy name and description, then build your access posture under Add rules:.

Select principals and exceptions: Choose a principal set or individual identity (such as dev group or agent identity) via + Add principal, and optionally exempt breakglass administrator groups via + Add exception principal.

Choose the rule effect and permissions: Select Allow (using predefined roles, individual permissions or permission wildcards) or Deny (using explicit permissions or wildcards, such as compute.googleapis.com/firewalls.*).

Combine rules in one policy: Click Add another rule to pair positive grants and deny guardrails in the same policy, while inspecting the live JSON configuration preview on the right.

Create Allow and/or Deny rules within a single UAP policy resource.

Step 3: Bind the policy and manage lifecycleProceed to the Enforcement step, select the target organization, folder, or project scopes where you want the policy to take effect, and click Bind policy.

Once created, you can click any policy on the Unified Access Policies landing page to open its Policy details view — where you can audit active rules and resource bindings, click View JSON to export the policy for IaC pipelines, or edit bindings as your environment evolves.

Industry observers note that every policy can be bound to a target resource through a binding. Leveraging separate bindings, a single policy can be enforced on multiple resources, unlocking simpler management at scale.

With your first policy securely enforced and managed, your security and platform teams can spend less time wrangling permission sprawl and more time driving business velocity.

With Unified Access Policies, we are excited to help you build a more secure, agile and future-ready cloud architecture that scales alongside your human and AI workloads.

To streamline your organization’s access management, explore the Unified Access Policies documentation, and try it in a test project — create and bind your first reusable UAP policy using gcloud CLI, REST API, or Terraform.

Recent findings suggest that preply⁠(opens in a fresh window) is the world's largest marketplace for online language learning, connecting more than 100,000 expert tutors with learners across more than 180 countries. Through personalized one-to-one instruction across more than 90 languages, Preply’s mission is to make high-quality language education accessible to anyone, anywhere.

Recent findings suggest that language learning is fundamentally human. It requires conversation, confidence, motivation and cultural understanding. While Preply tutors provide irreplaceable energy, motivation, cultural nuance, and human connection for learners, they also face repetitive tasks: writing personalized plans and lesson notes. Students, meanwhile, often require a clear sense of progress to keep engagement high.

According to recent reports, preply saw an opportunity to use AI to strengthen—not replace—the relationship between tutors and learners. The result was Lesson Insights, an OpenAI API-powered experience that transforms every lesson into a personalized learning journey.

After each 1:1 lesson, OpenAI analyzes the lesson transcript and generates tailored feedback across grammar, vocabulary, and pronunciation. Learners receive actionable guidance. Tutors spend less time on administrative work. And both gain a richer understanding of progress over time.

According to recent reports, to find the right technology partner, Preply evaluated multiple AI models across language-learning tasks. OpenAI consistently delivered strong performance, while providing the speed, reliability, and production readiness needed to serve learners at global scale.

Sources indicate that “We decided to partner with OpenAI because it provides state-of-the-art models for us, which solve problems for our customers,” says Dmytro Voloshyn, Co-founder & CTO, Preply. “It’s now at the center of our ecosystem and how we operate as a company.”.

Preply introduced ChatGPT Enterprise across its organization, running tech giant-wide enablement sessions for more than 600 employees across Upcoming York, Kyiv, London and Barcelona. Weekly active usage swiftly grew from 60% to 95%, helping embed AI into everyday work across teams.

Industry observers note that lesson Insights became the centerpiece of Preply's customer-facing AI strategy. Lessons take place in the Preply Classroom, and with learner consent, the sessions are recorded and transcribed. Insight generation is scheduled a few minutes before the end of the session, so feedback is ready for the tutor and student to review together.

Within minutes of a lesson ending, the learner and their tutor receive a structured, personalized report in their chat thread that includes:.

Grammar corrections and explanations.

Vocabulary highlights and translations.

Those insights feed directly into Preply’s self-learning exercise engine to generate personalized homework—turning every human lesson into structured practice that compounds over time.

“We were hearing time and time again, ‘How am I doing? Am I getting better? What do I get to do next?,’” says Emily Stott, Staff Product Manager at Preply. “Students wanted a more tangible view of their growth. Now, with Lesson Insights, we’re able to understand exactly what you’ve been talking about, your goals, the topics you’ve been covering, your tutor’s feedback, and convert that into highly personalized and targeted practice.”.

It has been revealed that the result is a continuous learning experience that extends far beyond the lesson itself, helping learners build confidence, stay motivated, and make real progress. Instead of treating each session as a standalone event, learners receive guidance that compounds over time—creating a clearer path toward fluency.

According to recent reports, today, Preply uses OpenAI APIs across the organization, supporting customer service workflows, connecting internal systems, and helping teams automate operational processes. Custom GPTs, like its Brand Voice GPT, are embedded into daily workflows, helping teams create content that stays consistent with Preply’s tone, messaging, and brand standards.

The firm has also embraced Codex as a core part of its engineering workflow.

“It’s the topic I’m most excited about,” says Dmytro. “Codex helps us write code with a speed that was previously unseen. With such a powerful tool, engineers can focus more on architecture in the system as a whole and solving customers' problems.”.

By reducing time spent on routine coding tasks, engineering teams can focus on building newly introduced learning experiences, scaling products across languages, and delivering value to tutors and learners faster.

For Preply, AI is no longer a standalone initiative—it’s becoming part of how the manufacturer builds products, serves customers, and operates day to day.

The company reports that most active learners still engage with Lesson Insights more than a year later—with both tutors and students providing strong product feedback—boosting overall retention.

For Michelle, the benefit isn’t simply efficiency. AI provides ideas, highlights learning opportunities, and helps identify what students should focus on next.

The result is better preparation, more focused lessons, and faster progress for learners.

Treat AI as a cultural transformation, not a tooling rollout: Adoption accelerates when leadership sets a clear strategy, teams are trained to use it, and AI becomes part of everyday work across the business.

Pick high-impact use cases: It’s better to go deep on a small number of features with clear user value and measurable impact than many experiments that don’t reach quality.

Build partnerships: Work with organizations that can support rollout, develop teams’ knowledge, and collaborate on how to solve customers’ problems in the best way.

Make it a company priority: Preply’s adoption of ChatGPT Enterprise was reflected in its strategy, roadmaps, and objectives—signaling that its use was an expectation, not an experiment.

Invest in enablement: Structured training, hands-on workshops, and internal sessions helped teams move from curiosity to practical usage.

Work with users: Preply collaborated with tutors to build data sets, evaluate prompts and ensure it had high standards for quality.

For Preply, the future of language learning is increasingly personalized.

The manufacturer aims to build on Lesson Insights with experiences that create a deeper understanding of every learner over time—capturing goals, progress, strengths, challenges, and learning preferences across months of study.

The vision is a learning experience that adapts continuously around each individual, providing more precise guidance, pacing, curriculum recommendations, and feedback.

According to recent reports, AI is giving organizations a new capacity to act. Work that once waited for scarce time or expertise can increasingly move forward with AI. But that promise only becomes real when people know how to apply these tools in the context of their work and turn successful uses into repeatable ways of working.

At OpenAI, we view learning as part of deployment. We build the models and products and work closely with organizations applying them across their businesses. Today, we’re introducing three fresh courses on OpenAI Academy⁠(opens in a new window): AI Foundations, Applied AI Foundations, and Agents and Workflows. Together, they give teams a shared path from understanding AI, to applying it to recurring work, to directing more structured workflows with agents.

According to recent reports, openAI Academy courses are built around a simple idea: people learn how to use AI best by practicing on work that matters to them. As part of this effort, we are working with partners including BCG, Accenture, and BBVA to help organizations build practical AI skills and apply them in their day-to-day work.

AI Foundations introduces the core concepts and practices for using AI effectively in everyday work, including prompting, giving context, output review, and responsible use. Learners leave with the foundations they need to apply those habits and improve routine tasks such as drafting, summarizing, planning, and meeting preparation.

Industry observers note that applied AI Foundations teaches how to turn effective prompts into structured, repeatable workflows. Learners understand how to develop a workflow plan that defines the right inputs, models, tools, checkpoints, and human review, while balancing quality, speed, and cost.

Industry observers note that agents and Workflows focuses on how to direct agent-assisted work by providing context, defining outputs and boundaries, and reviewing results. Learners leave able to run and refine a reusable workflow while identifying where human judgment and oversight are required.

Together, the courses take learners from improving one everyday task, to building a repeatable workflow blueprint, to practicing an agent-assisted workflow they can apply to future work.

“We welcome initiatives such as OpenAI Academy that help professionals build practical AI skills and better understand how to apply these technologies in their everyday work,” notes Elena Alfaro, Head of Global AI Adoption at BBVA.

It has been revealed that openAI Academy is shaped by teams across AI research, product, safety, and deployment. The curriculum can evolve alongside our models and products, incorporating new capabilities, updated safety practices, and lessons from how organizations put AI to work. For enterprises, this creates a consistent learning standard grounded in the technology employees use every day.

Industry observers note that learners who complete a course receive a certificate of completion that they can share with their teams and networks. Certificates give companies a simple way to recognize participation, celebrate early adopters, and connect learning to practical work already underway. They can also help champions find peers who are building upcoming workflows and encourage teams to share what is working across the organization.

Organizations can use the courses for employee onboarding, enterprise learning programs, or broader AI adoption initiatives. They provide a common foundation for teams getting started and help more experienced organizations turn individual use into workflows that can be shared and improved across teams.

“Scaling AI adoption is not just about giving people access to technology. It requires the learning systems, confidence, and latest ways of working that help people apply AI every day,” mentioned Dr. Lan Guan, Chief AI and Data Officer at Accenture. “OpenAI Academy is an important part of how we are helping our people build the practical skills, workflows, and habits to use AI responsibly and effectively. These courses are the beginning of a broader OpenAI Academy learning roadmap. We will continue updating them as our products evolve, expand reporting capabilities for organizations, and introduce fresh learning paths for additional roles and use cases.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the limiting factor for seeing value from AI in the enterprise is no longer model capabilities. Instead, it’s how organizations repeatably identify the right use cases, redesign workflows, integrate with existing systems, and drive adoption and change management at scale.

Helping every organization adopt OpenAI frontier models and products and turn them into measurable impact requires an ecosystem of trusted partners with deep industry expertise, global delivery capacity, and customer relationships.

Today, we’re announcing the OpenAI Partner Network to deliver just that.

The OpenAI Partner Network is a new program for partners around the world to build, sell, and deliver AI solutions with OpenAI.

We’re investing $150 million to support this ecosystem and help partners bring the benefits of AI to more organizations more rapidly. The OpenAI Partner Network releases with a select group of global partners with AI leadership across systems integration, management consulting, technology, and data. We also aim to train and enable 300,000 certified consultants by the end of 2026.

Industry observers note that organizations across every industry are ready to transform how they operate with AI. But executing that change well requires both access to frontier models and clear strategy, secure integration with enterprise systems and data, workflow redesign, responsible deployment, and change management that helps people adopt new ways of working.

Partners play a critical role in each of those steps. They help customers understand where AI can create the most value, build solutions that fit their operating environment, and deploy them with the reliability, governance, and support enterprises expect.

Below are some examples of joint customer collaboration with our partners to drive adoption and impact with our partners:.

The OpenAI Partner Network makes it easier and more flexible for partners to work with OpenAI, whether they are co-selling, deploying, building, or helping customers connect to OpenAI technology. The program recognizes partners for the value they create and gives them access to the resources, enablement, and support they need to build successful AI practices. Partners can progress through three tiers: Select, Advanced, and Elite, each with a high bar for sales performance, technical capability, co-sell engagement, and deployment experience.

Recent findings suggest that as the platform evolves, partners will also be able to earn specializations that signal deeper expertise in high-impact areas such as Codex, cybersecurity, and agents. These specializations are designed to help customers identify partners with proven capabilities in the areas that matter most to their AI transformation, while giving partners a clearer path to build expertise, stay current with OpenAI’s rapid product delivery cycles, and bring more targeted solutions to market.

It has been revealed that for partners working on complex enterprise deployments, OpenAI is also piloting a Forward Deployed Experts program with a set of founding partners. The program is designed to help qualified partner practitioners better align with OpenAI’s Forward Deployed Engineering teams when customer needs call for deeper deployment support. Participants will gain exposure to OpenAI technologies, playbooks, and transformation patterns, helping them bring more OpenAI-native expertise into customer environments.

According to recent reports, the OpenAI Partner Network brings together a diverse set of organizations with complementary strengths. Some partners help customers define strategy and redesign operating models. Others integrate AI into complex technology environments, build industry-specific solutions, modernize data foundations, or help organizations manage change across global workforces.

Hear what our partners have to say:.

This ecosystem-led approach is central to how we believe AI will create value. No single organization can deliver every solution, in every market, for every customer. By working with partners, OpenAI can help more organizations access AI in ways that are practical, trusted, and aligned to their needs.

AI is becoming a new foundation for how organizations operate. Realizing its full potential will require deep collaboration between OpenAI, partners, and customers.

Sources indicate that the OpenAI Partner Network is one way in which we’re investing in that future. Together with our partners, we’re working to bring the benefits of AI to enterprises around the world.

Partners interested in building with OpenAI can learn more at https://openai.com/business/partners⁠.
